title: Collecting data
cover_sub: Classify data, design good survey questions, avoid bias in samples, and organise data in frequency tables, grouped tables and two-way tables.

parents.listen: Ask: would everyone answer this question the same way you meant it? For samples, ask: who is left out? These questions are about judgement as much as calculation, so it's worth talking through answers.

levels_long.d: Getting the basics: one step at a time.
levels_long.s: Year 8 standard: a few steps, some in context.
levels_long.e: A stretch: problems, reasoning and spotting mistakes.

briefing: Categorical data are words or categories (eye colour). Discrete data are counted and can only take certain values (number of siblings, shoe size). Continuous data are measured and can take any value (height, time).
A population is everyone you want to know about; a sample is the group you actually ask. A sample is biased if it isn't representative, for example asking only one year group or only people at a gym.
Good survey questions are clear, give a time frame, have response boxes that don't overlap and cover every answer, and don't lead people towards an answer.
Grouped data use class intervals such as 150 ≤ h < 160: from 150 up to, but not including, 160. A two-way table shows two kinds of information at once.

examples.question: Is each type of data categorical, discrete or continuous? Eye colour, number of siblings, height.
steps: Eye colour is described in words: categorical.
Siblings are counted, and there are no halves: discrete.
Height is measured and can be any value: continuous.

examples.question: Improve this survey question: How much TV do you watch? A lot / Some / A little
steps: 'A lot' means different things to different people, and there's no time frame.
Give a time frame and number boxes that don't overlap and cover every answer.
examples.answer: How many hours of TV did you watch yesterday? 0 to 1 · more than 1 up to 2 · more than 2 up to 3 · more than 3

examples.question: 30 students were asked how they travel to school. Complete the two-way table.
steps: Girls in total: 30 − 14 = 16. Girls who walk: 16 − 7 = 9.
examples.answer: Boys bus 6; girls walk 9, total 16; walk 17, bus 13

d.blurb: Warm up. One step at a time.

text: Is shoe size discrete or continuous?
questions.answer: Discrete: it only takes certain values (sizes and half sizes).

text: Is the time to run 100 m discrete or continuous?
questions.answer: Continuous: time is measured and can be any value.

text: The pets of 12 students: dog, cat, dog, fish, dog, cat, rabbit, dog, cat, dog, fish, dog.
Make a frequency table. Which pet is the most common?
questions.answer: Dog 6, cat 3, fish 2, rabbit 1. Dog is the most common (the mode).

text: A school has 800 students. Ana asks 50 of them about school lunches. What is the population, and what is the sample size?
questions.answer: The population is the 800 students; the sample size is 50.

text: What is wrong with these response boxes for How many books did you read last month? 0–5 · 5–10 · 10–15
questions.answer: They overlap (5 and 10 are in two boxes), and there's no box for more than 15.

text: Is favourite colour categorical, discrete or continuous?

s.blurb: The Year 8 standard. Show each step.

text: Complete the grouped frequency table.

Height h (cm)Frequency
140 ≤ h < 150
150 ≤ h < 160
160 ≤ h < 170
170 ≤ h < 180
Why is this a bad survey question? Write a better one. Don't you agree that school lunches are too expensive?
questions.answer: It's a leading question: it pushes people to agree. Better: What do you think of the price of school lunches? Too expensive / About right / Good value

text: To find out how much exercise people in a town do, Leo asks people leaving a gym. Explain why his sample is biased.
questions.answer: People leaving a gym probably exercise more than most people, so they don't represent the whole town.

text: 40 students choose football or drama. Complete the two-way table.

FootballDramaTotal
Boys12
Girls15
Total2040
questions.answer: Boys drama 5, boys total 17; girls football 8, girls total 23; drama total 20
questions.working: Drama total 40 − 20 = 20, so boys drama 20 − 15 = 5. Girls football 20 − 12 = 8.

text: A height of exactly 160 cm. Does it go in 150 ≤ h < 160 or 160 ≤ h < 170?
questions.working: < 160 means up to but not including 160.
questions.tip: ≤ means 'less than or equal to'; < means 'less than'.

text: Design a data collection sheet for how students in your class travel to school.
questions.answer: A table with a row for each way of travelling (walk, bus, car, bike, other), a tally column and a frequency column.

e.blurb: Problems, reasoning and one piece of tampered evidence.

text: Use your table from question 10. What fraction of the students who chose drama are girls? Simplify.
questions.working: 1520 = 34

text: Ella grouped times in minutes like this. Find the problem and write better groups.
questions.answer: 10 and 20 each fit two groups. Better: 0 ≤ t < 10, 10 ≤ t < 20, 20 ≤ t < 30

text: A head teacher wants students' views on the canteen. She plans to ask the first 20 students in the lunch queue. Give two reasons this sample might be biased, and suggest a better one.
questions.answer: They all use the canteen and arrived early, and 20 is small. Better: pick students at random from every year group, including those who don't use the canteen, and ask more of them.

text: 120 people were asked a question in a survey and 45% said yes. How many people said yes?

mistakes: Calling counted data continuous: anything you count (people, goals, shoe sizes) is discrete.
Response boxes that overlap (0–5, 5–10) or leave gaps, or no box for large answers.
Putting a boundary value in the wrong class: 160 belongs in 160 ≤ h < 170.
Saying a sample is biased 'because it's small'. Small samples are unreliable; biased samples leave groups out.
closed_points: Classify data as categorical, discrete or continuous.
Write fair survey questions and response boxes.
Spot bias in a sample and suggest a better one.
Use tally charts, grouped frequency tables and two-way tables.
